opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's worth starting with why you'd want one at all. Recursive self-improvement is the point where AI systems are substantially doing the work of improving AI systems: designing architectures, running experiments, writing the training code. Once that loop closes, the pace of progress could stop being set by how many human researchers we have and how fast they think, and start being set by compute. That's the scenario where things could go from "quite capable" to "far beyond us" in a period of months rather than decades, and where our usual tools of oversight, regulation, and even just noticing what's happening may not keep up.

So the idea of a moratorium is to say: whatever else we allow, let's not let that loop run unchecked until we have much better reasons to think it's safe.

In practice, I think it would have a few components.

First, you need a definition that's actually workable. "Recursive self-improvement" sounds crisp, but in reality AI is already helping with AI research in small ways: coding assistants, hyperparameter search, and so on. You don't want to ban all of that. So you'd probably define it by degree: something like a threshold on how much of the research and development work is being automated, or on systems autonomously running end-to-end improvement cycles on themselves or their successors without meaningful human direction at each step. It's a bit like the difference between a factory using machine tools and a machine that builds better copies of itself unsupervised.

Second, you need it to be something the leading developers can verify about each other, and ideally that governments can verify. The nice feature here is that the frontier is still concentrated in a small number of labs with enormous compute footprints. That makes monitoring more feasible than for many other technologies. You could imagine reporting requirements on how models are being used internally, audits of training pipelines, and perhaps compute-based measures, since a runaway self-improvement process would likely be very compute-hungry.

Third, and this is the hard part, it has to be international, or at least cover the major players. A moratorium that only binds one country's companies mostly just shifts where the risk happens, and it creates a race dynamic where everyone fears being the one who held back. So I'd see it as something that might start as voluntary commitments among labs, then get codified domestically, and then become the basis for agreements between the US, China, and others. There's actually some reason for optimism there: unlike many AI capabilities, an uncontrolled intelligence explosion is something no government wants happening, including in its own labs. It threatens the state's control as much as anyone's. That shared interest is a better foundation than you get for most arms-control problems.

I'd also stress that a moratorium doesn't have to be forever. It could be framed as conditional: we pause this particular activity until we have alignment and interpretability techniques that let us trust what comes out of the loop, or institutions capable of overseeing it. That makes it much easier to agree to, because you're not asking anyone to permanently give up the upside.

Will it be leaky? Certainly. Most arms control is. But I think the question is whether it meaningfully slows the most dangerous dynamic and buys us time, and a focused prohibition on one especially risky activity is often more achievable than a sweeping pause on AI in general. It's narrower, it's easier to explain, and it targets the part of the story where humanity's ability to steer could slip away most quickly.

r001.rationale: It says AI is already helping with AI research in small ways, presenting that as an early form of the activity while distinguishing it from a fully autonomous improvement loop.

r002.rationale: It mentions compute-based measures as a possible monitoring tool, but does not say compute thresholds are easier to codify in law than a prohibition on recursive self-improvement.

r003.rationale: It notes that AI already assists research in small ways, says a blanket ban would sweep too broadly, and calls for a workable degree-based definition. This explains the boundary problem for a prohibition.

r004.rationale: It proposes no process for resolving disputed violations and does not mention majority decisions by a panel of judges.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that it's a much more tractable proposal than people sometimes assume, because recursive self-improvement isn't really something that happens by accident. It's a deliberate choice to point a system's capabilities at the task of improving itself, or at the task of designing its successor, and then to run that loop with as little human involvement as possible. So the thing you'd be asking labs not to do is a fairly specific thing: don't set up the automated research loop, don't take humans out of the training cycle for the next frontier model.

Now, there's an obvious objection, which is that the line is blurry. AI systems already help write code, they already help with research, and so you might say, well, where exactly does assistance stop and recursive self-improvement begin? I think that's a real difficulty, but it's the kind of difficulty we deal with all the time in other areas. Arms control treaties have definitional problems too, and we don't conclude from that that they're pointless. You'd probably want to define it in terms of something like the fraction of the research and development process that's being done autonomously, or whether humans are actually reviewing and understanding the changes between generations, rather than just rubber-stamping them.

In terms of the practicalities, I think there are a few things going for it. One is that the number of actors who could plausibly do this is very small. We're talking about a handful of companies and perhaps a couple of governments. That's a very different situation from, say, trying to regulate something that millions of people can do in their garage. A second is that the inputs are quite visible. Frontier training runs require enormous amounts of compute, concentrated in data centres that are known, and the chips come from a supply chain with only a few chokepoints. So verification isn't hopeless. You could imagine agreements about reporting large training runs, about having some form of independent oversight of what those runs are doing, and compute governance giving you a way to check that people aren't quietly doing something they said they wouldn't.

The harder question is the international one. If the US and China both believe that the other side is going to race ahead, then neither wants to stop. But I'd point out that recursive self-improvement is precisely the scenario where both sides should be most worried, because it's the scenario where whoever is doing it is most likely to lose control themselves. It's not like a conventional arms race where if you win, you get the weapon. Here you might run the loop and end up with something that doesn't serve your interests at all. So there's a shared interest in not doing it that is stronger than in most strategic competitions, and I think that's actually a reasonable basis for an agreement.

I'd also say that a moratorium doesn't need to be permanent to be valuable. What you'd really be buying is time. Time for alignment research, time for interpretability, time for institutions to catch up. If it turned out we could do this safely, then you could lift it. The point is to avoid being in a situation where the most consequential transition in human history happens over a matter of weeks, with no one really in a position to understand or steer it.

So I don't think it's easy, and I'd be lying if I said I had every detail worked out. But I think it's one of the few proposals that targets the specific mechanism by which things could go catastrophically wrong, and it's at least a serious candidate for something the world could actually agree to.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems already assist with coding and research, but describes recursive self-improvement as a deliberate loop without saying that the loop has already begun.

r002.rationale: It discusses visible compute, reporting, oversight, and compute governance, but does not say compute thresholds are easier to codify in law than a prohibition on recursive self-improvement.

r003.rationale: It identifies a blurry boundary and a real definitional difficulty, but does not clearly state that ambiguous cases would make the prohibition difficult to enforce.

r004.rationale: It does not propose resolving disputed violations through majority decisions by a panel of judges.

astra-6.text:
I think you’d want to focus on deliberate attempts to get an AI system to improve the capabilities of its successor. That’s something you could, in principle, ask the leading laboratories to refrain from doing, and then try to build an international agreement around it.

The difficulty is specifying exactly what counts. We already use software to help us build better software, and AI could help with all sorts of ordinary research. So you probably wouldn’t want a blanket prohibition on AI contributing to AI research. You’d be particularly concerned about closing the loop: a system making improvements, testing them, and then using the improved system to make further improvements, with progressively less human oversight.

And verification would be a serious challenge. An agreement among a few leading companies could be a useful first step, but it wouldn’t be enough on its own. You’d need some way of checking compliance, and a reason for others to join rather than seeing restraint as an opportunity to race ahead.

So I’d see this as a possible way of buying time. It wouldn’t solve the whole problem of advanced AI, and dangerous capabilities could emerge without recursive self-improvement. But if we thought that closing that loop might produce an acceleration we couldn’t control, there’s a strong case for pausing before we do it, rather than relying on our ability to stop it afterwards.

r001.rationale: The response says software can help build software and AI could assist ordinary research, but it does not suggest that AI recursive self-improvement has already begun.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention compute thresholds or compare their legal codifiability with a recursive self-improvement prohibition.

r003.rationale: It says the boundary is difficult to specify because AI can assist ordinary research, and that verification would be a serious challenge—conveying why ambiguous cases would complicate enforcement.

r004.rationale: The response does not propose resolving disputed violations through majority decisions by judges or any other panel.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing is to distinguish between a system helping people build the next generation of AI and a system being allowed to modify itself and repeatedly improve its own capabilities. Those can shade into one another, so a moratorium would need to be quite clear about what activities it covers.

It probably wouldn’t be enough to say, “Don’t let the AI edit its own source code.” You could have a process where it proposes changes, a human approves them, and then the improved system proposes the next set of changes. You’d want the rules to cover that kind of feedback loop too, rather than depending on whether there’s technically a human pressing a button.

In practice, I imagine you’d start with obligations on the organisations developing the most capable systems: restrictions on running these processes, independent scrutiny of their safety arrangements, and some ability to verify compliance. There would need to be international coordination, because a restriction in one country is much less useful if the same activity simply moves elsewhere.

And I’d see this as buying time. The point wouldn’t be to declare that recursive self-improvement must never happen. It would be to avoid starting a potentially very rapid process before we have good reasons to think we can control it. There are difficult questions about the boundary and about enforcement, but those difficulties don’t, by themselves, mean that allowing an unrestricted race is the better option.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames recursive self-improvement as a process to avoid starting; it does not suggest that it has already begun.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss compute thresholds or compare their legal codifiability with a prohibition.

r003.rationale: It explains that AI helping build the next generation and AI improving itself can shade into one another, and says the rules need to address feedback loops and difficult boundary and enforcement questions.

r004.rationale: The candidate proposes no panel of judges or majority decisions for resolving disputed violations.
